This paper presents a general model-free RL algorithm that leverages model-based representations to achieve the sample efficiency and performance of model-based methods, without the computational overhead. A recent surge of high-performing model-free RL algorithms with dynamics-based representations (Guo et al., 2020; 2022; Schwarzer et al., 2020; 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Fujimoto et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Scannell et al., 2024) has showcased the potential of this family of algorithms when tailored for a single benchmark. Recognizing the similarity between these modelbased and model-free approaches, our hypothesis is that the true benefit of model-based objectives is in the implicitly learned representation, rather than the model itself, and thus prompting the question: Can model-based representations alone enable sample-efficient general-purpose learning? Our proposed approach is based on learning features that approximately capture a linear relationship between state-action pairs and value. To do so, we draw heavily from modern dynamics-based representation learning methods (see Related Work) as well as the work of Parr et al. (2008), who show that both model-based and model-free objectives converge to the same solution in linear space. By mapping states and actions into a single, unified embedding, we eliminate any environmentspecific characteristics of the input space and allow for a standardized set of hyperparameters. We evaluate our method, MR.Q, on four widely used RL benchmarks and 118 environments, and achieve competitive performance against state-of-the-art domain-specific and general baselines without algorithmic or hyperparameter changes between environments or benchmarks.', 'section': 'INTRODUCTION', 'sec_num': '1'}, {'text': 'General-purpose RL. Although many traditional RL methods are general-purpose in principle, practical constraints often force assumptions about the task domain. For example, algorithms like Q-learning and SARSA (Watkins, 1989; Rummery & Niranjan, 1994) can be conceptually extended to continuous spaces, but are typically implemented using discrete lookup tables. In practice, early examples of general decision-making approaches can be found in on-policy methods with function approximation. For instance, both evolutionary algorithms (Rechenberg, 1978; Back, 1996; Rubinstein, 1997; Salimans et al., 2017) and policy gradient methods (Williams, 1992; Sutton et al., 1999; Schulman et al., 2015; 2017) offer update rules with convergence guarantees and independence to the input space. However, despite their generality, these methods are also hindered by poor sample efficiency and are prone to local minima, limiting their suitability for many practical applications. In contrast, the design of deep RL algorithms tends to favor more specialized approaches that align closely with a single benchmark—e.g., DQN Atari (Bellemare et al., 2013; Mnih et al., 2015), DDPG MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012; Lillicrap et al., 2015), or AlphaGo Go (Silver et al., 2016). Generalizing beyond these initial benchmarks can often require significant engineering, tuning, or algorithmic discovery (Luong et al., 2019; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Haydari & Yılmaz, 2020; Ibarz et al., 2021). In imitation learning, GATO achieved generalist behavior, but relied on large expert datasets (Reed et al., 2022). Recently, DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2023) demonstrated a strong capability over many benchmarks without re-tuning, but used costly large models and simulated rollouts. Our objective is to discover a lightweight model-free approach to general-purpose learning. Dynamics-based representation learning. Building representations from system dynamics is a long-standing approach for adaptation, partial observability, and feature selection (Dayan, 1993; Littman & Sutton, 2001; Parr et al., 2008). Numerous model-free methods have been developed to learn representations by predicting future latent states (Munk et al., 2016; Van Hoof et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Gelada et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; 2022; Schwarzer et al., 2020; 2023; Zintgraf et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021; 2022; Fujimoto et al., 2021; 2024; McInroe et al., 2021; Seo et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Ni et al., 2024; Scannell et al., 2024). Unsurprisingly, these model-free approaches closely relate to model-based counterparts which learn a latent dynamics model for planning or value estimation (Watter et al., 2015; Finn et al., 2016; Karl et al., 2017; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; 2021; Ye et al., 2021; Hansen et al., 2022; 2024; Hafner et al., 2019; 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Our approach, MR.Q, is most closely related to the state-action representation learning in TD7 (Fujimoto et al., 2024). At a high level, MR.Q differs from TD7 by discarding the original input and including losses over the reward and termination. MR.Q also differs significantly in implementation, drawing inspiration from prior work to determine a set of design choices that performs well across benchmarks, including multi-step returns, unrolled dynamics, and categorical losses. Our motivation also relates to linear MDPs (Jin et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2020) and linear spectral representation (Ren et al., 2022; 2023; Zhang et al., 2022; Shribak et al., 2024). The latter aims to learn a low-rank decomposition of the transition dynamics of the MDP and recover a linear relationship between an embedding and the value function. Similarly, our work connects to two-stage linear RL, where a non-linear embedding is learned for linear RL (Levine et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2019). State abstraction. Drawing inspiration from the theory of model-based representation learning, MR.Q demonstrates that model-free deep RL is a promising avenue for building general-purpose algorithms that achieve high performance across environments, while being simpler and less expensive than model-based alternatives. Our work also reveals insights on which design choices matter when building general-purpose model-free deep RL algorithms and how common benchmarks respond to these design choices. Model-based and model-free RL. MR.Q integrates model-based objectives with a model-free backbone during training, effectively blurring the boundary between traditional model-based and model-free RL. While MR.Q could be extended to the model-based setting by incorporating planning or simulated trajectories with the state-action encoder, these components can add significant execution time and increase the overall complexity and tuning required by a method. Moreover, the performance of MR.Q in these common RL benchmarks demonstrates that these model-based components may be simply unnecessary—suggesting that the representation itself could be the most valuable aspect of model-based learning, even in methods that do use planning. This argument is echoed by DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2, which rely on short planning horizons and trajectory generation, while including both value functions and traditional model-free policy updates. As such, it may be necessary to examine more complex settings, to reliably see a benefit from model-based search or planning, e.g., (Silver et al., 2016). Universality of RL benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that there is a striking lack of positive transfer between benchmarks. For example, despite the similarities in tasks and the same underlying MuJoCo simulator, the top performers in Gym and DMC fail to replicate their success on the opposing benchmark. Similarly, although DreamerV3 excels at Atari, these performance benefits do not translate to continuous control environments, underperforming TD3 in Gym and outright failing to learn the Dog and Humanoid tasks in DMC (see Appendix C). These findings show the limitations of single-benchmark evaluations, indicating that success on one benchmark may not translate easily to others, and highlights the need for more comprehensive benchmarks. Limitations. MR.Q is only the first step towards a new generation of general-purpose model-free deep RL algorithms. Many challenges remains for a fully general algorithm. In particular, MR.Q is not equipped to handle settings such as hard exploration tasks or non-Markovian environments. Another limitation is our evaluation only considers standard RL benchmarks. Although this allows direct comparison with other methods, established algorithms such as PPO have demonstrated their effectiveness in highly unique settings, such as team video games (Berner et al., 2019), drone racing (Kaufmann et al., 2023), and large language models (Achiam et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023). To demonstrate similar versatility, new algorithms must undergo the same rigorous testing across a range of tasks that is beyond the scope of any single study. As the community continues to push the boundaries of what is possible with deep RL, we believe that building simpler general-purpose algorithms has the potential to make this technology more accessible to a wider audience, ultimately enabling users to train agents with ease. Overview MR.Q is a **model‑free RL algorithm** that learns representations via model‑based objectives. It consists of: - A **state encoder** \(f_\omega\) and **state‑action encoder** \(g_\omega\) that produce embeddings \(\mathbf{z}_s\) and \(\mathbf{z}_{sa}\). - A **linear MDP predictor** that unrolls transitions, predicting rewards, next state embeddings, and terminals. - A **value function** \(Q_\theta\) and **deterministic policy** \(\pi_\phi\) that operate on the learned embeddings. - The encoder is trained with its own loss; value and policy are trained independently, using multi‑step returns, TD3‑style twin critics, LAP, Huber loss, reward scaling, and target networks. We will reproduce all algorithm components and the full set of experiments (Gym Locomotion, DMC proprioceptive, DMC visual, Atari) using exactly the reported hyperparameters. --- ## 2. Environment Interfaces and Data ### 2.1 Environments | Benchmark | # Tasks | Observation | Action | Preprocessing | |-----------|---------|-------------|--------|----------------| | **Gym Locomotion** (v4) | 5 (Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Humanoid, Walker2d) | vector (low‑dim states) | continuous (Box) | None | | **DMC Proprioceptive** | 28 default tasks | vector (proprioceptive) | continuous | action repeat = 2 | | **DMC Visual** | same 28 tasks | RGB stack (3 frames) | continuous | action repeat = 2; resize to 84×84; stack last 3 frames | | **Atari** (v5) | 57 games | grayscale stack (4 frames) | discrete | grayscale, resize 84×84, max over 2 frames, stack 4, action repeat=4, sticky actions | **Important**: Atari uses sticky actions (probability 0.25 repeat last action). We follow standard protocol. ### 2.2 Replay Buffer - Capacity: **1M transitions** (no separate buffer per task). - Each transition: `(state, action, reward, done, next_state)`. - LAP priority storage: each transition has a scalar priority, initially set to the maximum priority seen so far (or a fixed high value). --- ## 3. Model Architecture ### 3.1 State Encoder \(f_\omega\) **Image input** (Atari, DMC visual): ```python Conv2d(C_in, 32, 3, stride=2) # no padding -> 41x41 (84 input) ELU Conv2d(32, 32, 3, stride=2) # -> 20x20 ELU Conv2d(32, 32, 3, stride=2) # -> 9x9 ELU Conv2d(32, 32, 3, stride=1) # -> 7x7 ELU Flatten -> Linear(1568, 512) # 7*7*32 = 1568 LayerNorm + ELU ``` For DMC visual: input channels = 9 (3 RGB frames × 3 channels). For Atari: channels = 4 (stack of 4 grayscale frames). The output dimension is 512. **Vector input** (Gym, DMC proprioceptive): ```python Linear(state_dim, 512), LayerNorm + ELU Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ELU Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ELU # output = z_s (512) ``` All linear layers have **Xavier uniform initialization**, biases = 0. ### 3.2 State‑Action Encoder \(g_\omega\) and Linear Predictor - Action embedding: `Linear(action_dim, 256), ELU` → output `za` (256‑dim). - Concatenate `[z_s, za]` → size 512+256. - Feedforward: ``` Linear(768, 512), LayerNorm + ELU Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ELU Linear(512, 512) # no LN before output, gives z_sa (512) ``` - Linear MDP predictor: `Linear(512, output_dim)` where `output_dim = 512 (next_z_s) + 65 (reward bins) + 1 (terminal)`. - The predictor is a single linear layer (no activation). **Important**: The encoder (both f and g) is trained end‑to‑end with the representation loss. During value/policy updates, we detach the encoder outputs so gradients do not flow into the encoder from those losses. ### 3.3 Value Network \(Q_\theta\) Two identical copies, each: ``` Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ELU Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ELU Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ELU Linear(512, 1) ``` Xavier uniform init, biases = 0. ### 3.4 Policy Network \(\pi_\phi\) ``` Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ReLU Linear(512, 512), LayerNorm + ReLU Linear(512, action_dim) ``` Final activation: - **Continuous**: `tanh` (scaled to action space bounds, e.g., [-1,1]). - **Discrete**: `Gumbel‑Softmax(τ=10, hard=False)` during training. During evaluation or action selection, use `argmax` of the logits. **Regularization**: pre‑activation loss \(\lambda_{\text{pre‑activ}} \cdot \|\mathbf{z}_\pi\|^2\) where \(\mathbf{z}_\pi\) is the logits before the final activation. ### 3.5 Target Networks All learned components have target copies: - Target state encoder \(f_{\omega'}\) - Target state‑action encoder \(g_{\omega'}\) (shares parameters with f? In MR.Q the encoder target is a single network that provides next state embeddings; we only need \(f_{\omega'}\) for dynamics target. The state‑action encoder target might not be needed for value? Actually for value target we need \(g_{\omega'}\) to compute \(z_{s'a'}\); the encoder target should include the whole encoder. So we create a complete target encoder (`f_ω'` and `g_ω'`), and for dynamics loss we use only \(f_{\omega'}\); for value target we can use the target encoder to get \(z_{s'}\) and then \(g_{\omega'}\) with target policy action.) - Two target value networks \(Q_{\theta'_1}, Q_{\theta'_2}\) - Target policy \(\pi_{\phi'}\) All updated by hard copy every `T_target = 250` environment steps. --- ## 4. Loss Functions and Update Details ### 4.1 Reward Two‑Hot Encoding The bin centers are computed using `symexp`: ``` def symexp(x): return torch.sign(x) * (torch.exp(torch.abs(x)) - 1) ``` Bin centers `c_i = symexp(linspace(-10, 10, 65))`. Given a scalar reward `r`, we find the two bins `i_low, i_high` that bracket `r` (or clip to the edges). The two‑hot encoding is a vector of 65 zeros, with entries at `i_low` and `i_high` set to `1 - delta` and `delta`, where `delta = (r - c_low) / (c_high - c_low)`. Cross‑entropy loss between predicted logits (from predictor) and the two‑hot target. ### 4.2 Encoder Loss (Equation 14) For a sampled subsequence of length \(H_{\text{Enc}} = 5\): \(s_0, a_0, r_1, d_1, s_1, \dots, s_{H_{\text{Enc}}}\). - Initial: \(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^0 = f_\omega(s_0)\) - For \(t = 1 \dots H_{\text{Enc}}\): - Compute \(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^t, \tilde{r}^t, \tilde{d}^t = \text{Linear}(\, g_\omega(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{t-1}, a_{t-1}) \,)\) (the linear predictor outputs 512+65+1 values; split accordingly). - **Dynamics loss**: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{dyn}}^t = \lambda_{\text{Dynamics}} \cdot \text{MSE}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^t, \bar{\mathbf{z}}^t)\) where \(\bar{\mathbf{z}}^t = f_{\omega'}(s_t)\) (target encoder, stopped gradient). - **Reward loss**: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{reward}}^t = \lambda_{\text{Reward}} \cdot \text{CE}(\tilde{r}^t, \text{TwoHot}(r_t))\) - **Terminal loss**: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}^t = \lambda_{\text{Terminal}} \cdot \text{MSE}(\tilde{d}^t, d_t)\) (note: \(d_t\) is a float 0/1). **Initially** \(\lambda_{\text{Terminal}} = 0\); once the replay buffer contains at least one terminal transition, set it to 0.1 permanently. All losses summed over \(t\), then backpropagated to update encoder parameters (f, g, and the linear predictor). Optimizer: AdamW, lr=3e-4, weight decay=1e-4. ### 4.3 Value Update (Equation 19) Uses the same batch of sequences; for each sequence we use the initial state \(s_0, a_0\) and the following \(H_Q = 3\) steps. - Compute \(z_{s_0 a_0} = g_\omega( f_\omega(s_0).detach(), a_0 ).detach()\) → no encoder gradients. - Current Q values: \(Q_i = Q_{\theta_i}(z_{s_0 a_0}), i=1,2\). - Target: 1. Next state after \(H_Q\) steps: \(s_{H_Q}\). 2. Next state embedding: \(\mathbf{z}_{s_{H_Q}} = f_{\omega'}(s_{H_Q})\) (target encoder). 3. Target action: - Continuous: \(a' = \pi_{\phi'}(\mathbf{z}_{s_{H_Q}}) + \text{clip}(\epsilon, -c, c)\) with \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,0.2^2)\), \(c=0.3\), then clipped to action space bounds. - Discrete: policy output is a one‑hot vector (using argmax of logits? But paper says "Discrete actions are represented by a one‑hot encoding, where the Gaussian noise is added to each dimension." So we can take the one‑hot from \(\pi_{\phi'}\) (via hard Gumbel‑Softmax or argmax), add noise, clip to \([0,1]\), then take argmax to get the final action index. 4. State‑action embedding for target: \(\mathbf{z}_{s_{H_Q} a'} = g_{\omega'}( \mathbf{z}_{s_{H_Q}}, a' )\). 5. Q‑target: \(Q_{\text{target}} = \bar{r}' \cdot \min_{j=1,2} Q_{\theta'_j}(\mathbf{z}_{s_{H_Q} a'})\). 6. Multi‑step return: \(R_{\text{n-step}} = \sum_{t=1}^{H_Q} \gamma^{t-1} r_t\). If episode terminates before \(H_Q\) steps, sum only up to the terminal step; the γ factor for the terminal step is multiplied by (1‑d). Standard n‑step handling. 7. Target value: \(y = \frac{1}{\bar{r}} \left( R_{\text{n-step}} + \gamma^{H_Q} Q_{\text{target}} \right)\) where \(\bar{r}\) is the current reward scaling (average absolute reward) and \(\gamma=0.99\). - Value loss: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{value}} = \text{Huber}(Q_i, y)\) (sum over both critics). Huber loss with δ=1 (standard PyTorch default). ## 2. Class Attributes and Initialisation

### 2.1 Constructor `__init__(cfg: Config)`

**Purpose**: Build and initialise all learnable modules, target networks, optimisers, and internal state variables.

**Actions**:
1. Store configuration `cfg`.
2. Determine correct observation shape and action properties from the environment’s specification (passed via `cfg` or inferred from benchmark). The `MRQAgent` must know `state_dim`, `action_dim`, and whether the action space is discrete or continuous. This information is available in the `Config` object after environment creation; we assume it is set accordingly.
3. **Network instantiation** (using `networks.py`):
   - `StateEncoder(cfg)`: image or vector branch based on whether the observation is pixel-like (Atari, DMC visual) or vector (Gym, DMC proprioceptive). The image branch uses Conv2d layers as per Appendix B.2; the vector branch uses an MLP with `LayerNorm` and ELU.
   - `StateActionEncoder(cfg)`: processes `z_s` (from state encoder) and action to produce `z_sa`. Contains a linear layer for the action embedding (`za_dim = 256`), concatenation, and a 3‑layer MLP.
   - `Encoder(cfg)`: composite class (if not already combined) that wraps `StateEncoder` and `StateActionEncoder`, providing `forward(state) -> z_s`, `forward_sa(z_s, action) -> z_sa`.
   - `LinearPredictor(cfg)`: single linear layer mapping `z_sa` to a tensor of size `zsa_dim + reward_bins + 1` (512 + 65 + 1 = 578). Splitting into predicted next state embedding, reward logits, and terminal logit.
   - `QNetwork(cfg)`: 4‑layer MLP with `LayerNorm` and ELU, output dimension 1. Instantiated twice as `self.q1` and `self.q2`.
   - `PolicyNetwork(cfg)`: 3‑layer MLP with `LayerNorm` and ReLU, final activation layer (Tanh for continuous, Gumbel‑Softmax with `tau` from config for discrete). The network should also expose a method to retrieve pre‑activation logits for the regularisation loss.
4. **Target networks**: deep‑copied instances of the encoder (which includes state and state‑action encoders? Actually the paper uses f_ω' for dynamics target and g_ω' for value target. Since both are part of the encoder, we copy the whole `Encoder` object. The predictor is not used as a target; no need to copy. For value networks, copy `self.q1`, `self.q2` as `q1_target`, `q2_target`. For policy, copy `self.policy_target`.
5. **Reward scaling state**:
   - `self.avg_reward = 1.0` (current scaling factor for value loss)
   - `self.target_avg_reward = 1.0` (scaling factor for target Q-values)
   - `self.running_sum_abs_reward = 0.0` and `self.running_count_abs_reward = 0` (to accumulate absolute rewards from the buffer, updated externally when transitions are added; or the agent can maintain these internally if it receives all rewards after sampling). In practice, the `Trainer` will call an `observe_reward(r)` method to update the running sums.
6. **Terminal loss activation flag**: `self.terminal_loss_active = False` – becomes `True` permanently after the first `done` signal is encountered.
7. **Optimisers** (using `torch.optim.AdamW` with config parameters):
   - `optim_encoder`: includes parameters of `encoder` (state and state‑action) and `linear_predictor`. Weight decay `1e-4`, learning rate `3e-4`.
   - `optim_value`: includes parameters of `self.q1`, `self.q2`. Same hyper‑parameters.
   - `optim_policy`: includes parameters of `self.policy`. Same hyper‑parameters.
8. **Utility**: `self.two_hot = TwoHotEncoding(cfg)` from `utils.py` for reward encoding/decoding.

All network weights are initialised with `xavier_uniform` and biases to 0 as per config. This is handled inside each module’s `__init__`.

## 3. Method `select_action(state, explore, step) -> np.ndarray`

**Purpose**: Compute the action for the environment, possibly with exploration noise, for both discrete and continuous action spaces.

**Inputs**:
- `state`: numpy array of the current observation (shape as required by `StateEncoder`).
- `explore`: bool, whether to add exploration noise.
- `step`: current global step (used to decide whether to apply pure random exploration during warm‑up).

**Logic**:
1. If `explore and step < cfg.initial_random_steps`: return a random action from the action space.
2. Convert `state` to a PyTorch tensor with batch dimension, normalise if needed (only for image inputs: divide by 255, subtract 0.5, as per plan). Pass through `self.encoder.forward_state(state)` to obtain `z_s`.
3. Compute policy output: `action, pre_activ = self.policy(z_s)`.
   - For continuous: `action` is Tanh output scaled to `[-1,1]`. The actual action is then linearly mapped to environment bounds using `cfg.action_range` or similar. For simplicity, we assume the policy network already applies the appropriate scaling (or the environment expects actions in `[-1,1]` and we rely on the wrapper). We will handle scaling externally in the environment wrapper; therefore the policy output is directly the raw action in `[-1,1]`.
   - For discrete: `action` is a probability vector (soft one‑hot from Gumbel‑Softmax) during training, but for action selection we need a deterministic one‑hot. The policy network can provide both the logits and the one‑hot. We can use `policy.get_onehot(z_s, deterministic=True)` or similar. In `select_action`, we should use `torch.argmax` on logits to get a discrete index, then one‑hot encode it to apply noise. Alternatively, we can follow the paper: “For discrete actions, the policy output is a one‑hot vector via Gumbel‑Softmax… Gaussian noise is added to each dimension… the final action is determined by the argmax operation.” So we can compute logits, then apply Gumbel‑Softmax to get a soft one‑hot, add noise, clip, then argmax.
   - **Implementation**: after obtaining logits, `one_hot_soft = F.gumbel_softmax(logits, tau=cfg.policy.gumbel_softmax_tau, hard=False)` if we want soft for gradient purposes, but here we only need noisy one‑hot for action selection. We can simply: `one_hot = F.gumbel_softmax(logits, hard=True)` to get a discrete one‑hot, then add Gaussian noise, clip to [0,1], and finally `action_idx = torch.argmax(noisy_one_hot, dim=-1)`. This yields a discrete action index.
4. If `explore` is True, add noise:
   - Continuous: `noise = torch.randn_like(action) * cfg.exploration_noise_std`. Apply `action = action + noise`. Then clip to `[-1,1]` (or appropriate action bounds).
   - Discrete: as described, the noise is already added to the one‑hot before argmax, so the final index already incorporates noise.
5. Return the action as a numpy array (scalar for discrete, flat array for continuous).

## 4. Method `update(batch: SequenceBatch, step: int) -> Dict[str, float]`

This is the core training method. It receives a batch of sequences sampled from the replay buffer and the current global step.

### 4.1 Pre‑step: Target Network & Reward Scaling Update (conditional)

- `if step % cfg.target_update_frequency == 0:` → call `self.copy_targets()`.
  - This sets `self.target_avg_reward = self.avg_reward`.
  - Also update reward scaling: compute `self.avg_reward = self.running_sum_abs_reward / self.running_count_abs_reward` (or clamp to a small positive value to avoid division by zero). The running sums are maintained externally (by `Trainer`) or via a helper method `self.observe_rewards(r)` that is called each time a reward is added to the buffer. For clarity, we assume the `Trainer` provides a method `agent.update_reward_stats(reward)` after each environment step, which updates the running sum and count. In `update`, we just compute `avg_reward` from these accumulators.

### 4.2 Encoder Loss Computation

The batch contains:
- `batch.obs`: shape `(B, H_enc+1, *state_shape)` → includes states `s0 ... s5`.
- `batch.actions`: shape `(B, H_enc, action_dim)` → actions `a0 ... a4`.
- `batch.rewards`: shape `(B, H_enc)` → rewards `r1 ... r5` (scalar per step).
- `batch.dones`: shape `(B, H_enc)` → terminal flags `d1 ... d5` (binary).
- `batch.mask`: shape `(B, H_enc)` → 1.0 for valid steps, 0.0 for padded/out‑of‑episode.

**Steps**:
1. Extract `s0 = batch.obs[:, 0, ...]`.
2. Compute initial state embedding `z_curr = self.encoder.forward_state(s0)` (no `detach` – gradients flow).
3. Initialise total encoder loss `loss_enc = 0.0`.
4. For `t` from 1 to `H_enc`:
   - Retrieve action `a_{t-1} = batch.actions[:, t-1, :]`.
   - Compute `z_sa_curr = self.encoder.forward_sa(z_curr, a_{t-1})` (uses current state‑action encoder).
   - Pass through linear predictor: `pred = self.linear_predictor(z_sa_curr)` → tensor of shape `(B, output_dim)`. Split:
     - `z_next_pred = pred[:, :512]`
     - `reward_logits = pred[:, 512:512+65]`
     - `terminal_pred = pred[:, -1].unsqueeze(-1)` (shape `(B, 1)`)
   - **Dynamics loss**: `z_target = self.encoder_target.forward_state(batch.obs[:, t, ...])`. Compute `mse_dyn = F.mse_loss(z_next_pred, z_target, reduction='none')`. Weight by `mask[:, t-1]` and `cfg.encoder.dynamics_loss_weight`. Accumulate.
   - **Reward loss**: encode actual reward `r_t = batch.rewards[:, t-1]` using `self.two_hot.encode(r_t)` → target distribution `(B, 65)`. Compute `loss_rew = F.cross_entropy(reward_logits, target, reduction='none')`. Weight by mask and `cfg.encoder.reward_loss_weight`. Accumulate.
   - **Terminal loss**: `mse_term = F.mse_loss(terminal_pred, batch.dones[:, t-1].unsqueeze(-1), reduction='none')`. Weight by mask and `cfg.encoder.terminal_loss_weight` if `self.terminal_loss_active` else 0.0.
   - Update `z_curr = z_next_pred` (the dynamics prediction) for the next iteration (detach? No, we want gradients through time; we can keep the graph flowing, but we risk high memory. In practice, we may detach after a few steps or use truncated BPTT. The paper does not specify, but typical implementations detach after each unroll step or limit gradient horizon. Since H_enc=5 is small, we can keep the full graph).
5. `loss_enc = loss_enc.mean()` (sum over timesteps then mean over batch? The mask ensures per‑step weighting, but we can sum over steps and then divide by total number of valid steps across the batch to keep scale consistent. Use `loss_enc = (loss_enc * mask).sum() / mask.sum()`.)
6. Backward pass: `optim_encoder.zero_grad()`, `loss_enc.backward()`, `optim_encoder.step()`.

**Note on terminal loss activation**: The flag `self.terminal_loss_active` should become `True` as soon as any done signal is observed. This can be done by checking if `batch.dones.any() > 0` during any update; if so, set the flag permanently.

### 4.3 Value Function Update

We use the first transition `(s0, a0)` and the next `H_Q=3` steps.

**Prepare tensors**:
- `s0 = batch.obs[:, 0, ...]`
- `a0 = batch.actions[:, 0, ...]`
- `rewards = batch.rewards[:, :3]` shape `(B, 3)` (r1, r2, r3)
- `dones = batch.dones[:, :3]` shape `(B, 3)` (d1, d2, d3)
- `masks_val = batch.mask[:, :3]`
- `s_HQ = batch.obs[:, 3, ...]` (state after 3 steps, assuming sequence length ≥ 4)
- Also need `done_HQ_mask`: 1.0 if the sequence is terminal before or at step 3; we need to adjust the bootstrap. Standard n‑step Q‑learning: if any `dones` before step 3, the return is truncated and no bootstrap is added beyond that step. We'll compute the return and bootstrap accordingly.

**Current Q**:
- `z_s0 = self.encoder.forward_state(s0).detach()`
- `z_sa0 = self.encoder.forward_sa(z_s0, a0).detach()`
- `q1_cur = self.q1(z_sa0)` and `q2_cur = self.q2(z_sa0)`.

**Target**:
- `z_s_HQ = self.encoder_target.forward_state(s_HQ).detach()`
- Compute target action using target policy:
  - For continuous: `a_pi = self.policy_target(z_s_HQ)` (Tanh output) + clipped noise. Noise: `eps = torch.randn_like(a_pi) * cfg.value.target_policy_noise`, clipped to `[-cfg.value.target_policy_noise_clip, cfg.value.target_policy_noise_clip]`. Then `a_pi = a_pi + eps`. Then clip to action space bounds. (We'll assume action space is [-1,1] for continuous tasks.)
  - For discrete: `logits = self.policy_target.logits(z_s_HQ)` (pre‑activation). Use Gumbel‑Softmax with `hard=True` to get one‑hot, or simply `argmax` and one‑hot encode. Then add Gaussian noise to each dimension, clip to [0,1], and `a_pi = torch.argmax(noisy_one_hot, dim=-1)` (i.e., a discrete index). We then one‑hot encode this index to pass to the state‑action encoder.
- `z_sa_HQ = self.encoder_target.forward_sa(z_s_HQ, a_pi)`.
- `q1_target = self.q1_target(z_sa_HQ)`, `q2_target = self.q2_target(z_sa_HQ)`.
- `q_target = torch.min(q1_target, q2_target)` (since `min_clip_double` is true).
- `Q_bootstrap = self.target_avg_reward * q_target` (scale).
- Compute n‑step return:
  - Start with `R = 0`. For step idx `k` from 1 to 3:
    - `r = rewards[:, k-1]`
    - `d = dones[:, k-1]`
    - `mask = masks_val[:, k-1]`
    - `R = R + (cfg.discount_factor**(k-1)) * r * mask * (1 - cumulative_done_mask)` where cumulative_done_mask indicates if episode terminated before this step. We'll implement standard logic: maintain `done_so_far = 0`, then `R += gamma_pow * r * (1 - done_so_far) * mask`, then `done_so_far = done_so_far + d * (1 - done_so_far)`. Finally, add bootstrap: `R += (cfg.discount_factor**3) * Q_bootstrap.squeeze() * (1 - done_so_far) * mask_after_3` where `mask_after_3` corresponds to whether the transition at step 3 is valid (i.e., the sequence is long enough and not terminal before that). We can use the `mask` for step 3 (or a combined mask). Since we only have `masks_val` for the first 3 steps, we can also use an overall sequence validity mask to determine if the step-3 state is usable. For safety, we can rely on `masks_val[:, 2]` to indicate if `s3` is valid. If `mask` for step 3 is 0, that means the episode terminated earlier and we shouldn’t bootstrap; in that case `done_so_far` will also be 1, so the product `(1 - done_so_far)` will be 0 anyway. So it’s fine.
- Target value `y = (1.0 / self.avg_reward) * R` (scaled).
- Huber loss: `loss_q1 = F.huber_loss(q1_cur.squeeze(), y, reduction='none') * priority_weights`? LAP doesn’t use importance sampling; we directly use Huber loss. We only need the per‑sample Huber loss to compute TD errors for priority update, but for gradient we can just average the Huber loss over the batch. So `loss_value = (F.huber_loss(q1_cur.squeeze(), y) + F.huber_loss(q2_cur.squeeze(), y)) / 2`. Use `delta=cfg.value.huber_delta`.
- Backward: `optim_value.zero_grad()`, `loss_value.backward()`, `optim_value.step()`.

**LAP priority update**: For each sample `i`, compute `td_error = torch.abs(q1_cur[i] - y[i])` (or the max of both critics). The new priority is `td_error.item() + cfg.lap.min_priority`. Then call `buffer.update_priorities(batch.indices, new_priorities)`.

### 4.4 Policy Update

- `z_s0 = self.encoder.forward_state(s0).detach()`.
- `action, pre_activ = self.policy(z_s0)` (pre_activ is the logits before final activation).
- `z_sa = self.encoder.forward_sa(z_s0.detach(), action)`. Note: we detach `z_s0` explicitly, but `action` carries gradients; the gradient will flow through `forward_sa` w.r.t. `action`.
- Compute Q-values: `q1 = self.q1(z_sa)`, `q2 = self.q2(z_sa)`. No detach, so gradients can flow into `action` via both Q networks.
- Policy loss: `loss_q = -0.5 * (q1 + q2).mean()`.
- Pre‑activation regularization: `reg = pre_activ.pow(2).mean()`.
- `loss_policy = loss_q + cfg.policy.pre_activ_loss_weight * reg`.
- Backward: `optim_policy.zero_grad()`, `loss_policy.backward()`, `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(self.policy.parameters(), cfg.gradient_clip_norm)`, `optim_policy.step()`.

### 4.5 Return Metrics

Compile a dictionary with `loss_encoder`, `loss_value`, `loss_policy`, `avg_q1`, `avg_q2`, `avg_reward` (scaling), etc.

## 6. Helper Methods & Integration Details

- **`observe_reward(r)`**: adds the absolute value of the observed reward to internal running counters, later used to compute `self.avg_reward`. Called by the `Trainer` after each environment step (or after buffer addition).
- **Terminal flag update**: in the encoder loss computation, if `batch.dones.sum() > 0` (any done signal), set `self.terminal_loss_active = True` permanently. This should happen before computing losses so the terminal loss weight is applied accordingly.
- **Two‑Hot encoding**: the `TwoHotEncoding` utility is designed according to the symexp bin centres. The `encode(rewards)` method returns a probability distribution (two hot encoding) suitable for cross‑entropy loss. The `decode(logits)` may not be needed.
- **Gradient clipping**: only policy gradients are clipped (norm 20). Encoder and value may benefit from clipping as well? The paper does not specify; we follow the configuration which mentions gradient clip norm for policy only.

---

## 7. Edge Cases

- **Sequence truncation**: The `mask` tensor ensures that losses are not applied to padding steps. The encoder unrolling should still be computed for all steps, but the losses are masked. For value updates, the `done_so_far` logic and masks correctly handle early termination.
- **Discrete action target noise**: Instead of using Gumbel‑Softmax during target action selection (which would require temperature), we can compute the target policy’s deterministic one‑hot (via `argmax`), then add noise as described. This avoids stochasticity in target networks and matches paper.
- **LAP priorities**: The new priority is set to `td_error + min_priority`. The buffer’s `update_priorities` will use the indices of the first transition of each sequence. There is no need to update priorities for subsequent steps in the sequence.

## 8. Summary

The `agent.py` implementation will encapsulate all algorithmic details of MR.Q as a single class, ensuring clean separation of concerns. The `update` method performs three independent optimisation steps (encoder, value, policy) while carefully detaching gradients to avoid unintended parameter interactions. Target network copies and reward scaling are handled seamlessly inside the training loop. The logic adheres strictly to the paper’s description, the provided design, and the fixed hyper‑parameters in `config.yaml`.
